spec.title: Blink an LED with an Arduino

steps.text: Connect pin D13 on the Arduino to one end of the 220 Ω resistor.
steps.tip: A resistor works either way round.

steps.text: Connect the other end of the resistor to the LED's long leg (+, the anode).
steps.tip: The resistor limits the current so the LED doesn't burn out.

steps.text: Connect the LED's short leg (−, the cathode) to GND on the Arduino.
steps.tip: The flat edge on the LED's rim marks the short leg.

steps.text: Plug in the USB cable and upload the code. The LED should blink once a second.

safety: Unplug the USB cable before changing any wires.
Double-check 5V and GND are never wired directly together (a short circuit).
Never connect an LED without a resistor; it can burn out the LED or the pin.
spec.videoQuery: arduino blink external led resistor beginner

spec.title: Read a push button with an Arduino

steps.text: Connect pin D2 to one leg of the button.
Connect the diagonally opposite leg to GND.
steps.tip: Using diagonal legs makes sure you go across the switch, not along a leg that's always connected.

steps.text: Upload the code and open the Serial Monitor: pressing the button prints "pressed".
steps.tip: INPUT_PULLUP uses the Arduino's built-in resistor, so no extra resistor is needed.

safety: Unplug the USB cable before changing any wires.
Double-check 5V and GND are never wired directly together (a short circuit).

spec.title: Control a servo motor with an Arduino

steps.text: Connect the servo's brown/black wire to GND.
steps.tip: Connect ground first; it's a good habit.

steps.text: Connect the red wire to 5V.
Connect the orange/yellow signal wire to pin D9.
Upload the code: the servo sweeps from 0° to 180° and back.

safety: Unplug the USB cable before changing any wires.
Double-check 5V and GND are never wired directly together (a short circuit).
One small servo is fine on USB power; for bigger or multiple servos use a separate 5V supply with a shared ground.

spec.title: Read a potentiometer (knob) with an Arduino

steps.text: Connect the left leg to 5V.
Connect the right leg to GND.
Connect the middle leg to A0.
steps.tip: The middle leg's voltage changes as you turn the knob; A0 measures it as 0–1023.

steps.text: Upload the code and open the Serial Monitor; turn the knob to see the number change.

safety: Unplug the USB cable before changing any wires.
Double-check 5V and GND are never wired directly together (a short circuit).

spec.title: Measure distance with an HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor

steps.tip: Trig sends out a sound pulse.

steps.tip: Echo reports how long the pulse took to bounce back.

spec.title: Light an LED from a Raspberry Pi

steps.text: Shut down the Pi and unplug its power.
Connect physical pin 11 (GPIO17) to one end of the 330 Ω resistor.
steps.tip: Pin 1 is the corner pin next to the square solder pad; numbers go 1, 2 across, then down.

steps.text: Connect the resistor's other end to the LED's long leg.
Connect the LED's short leg to physical pin 6 (GND).
Power the Pi back on and run the Python script.

safety: Raspberry Pi pins are 3.3V only: never connect 5V to a GPIO pin.
Power off before wiring.
spec.videoQuery: raspberry pi gpio led gpiozero beginner

code.source:
from gpiozero import LED
from time import sleep

led = LED(17)
while True:
    led.toggle()
    sleep(1)

spec.title: Read temperature with a DHT11 sensor module

steps.text: Connect the module's + pin to 5V and − pin to GND.
Connect the OUT/DATA pin to D2.
steps.tip: 3-pin modules already include the pull-up resistor; a bare 4-pin sensor needs a 10 kΩ resistor from DATA to 5V.

steps.text: Install the "DHT sensor library" in the Arduino IDE, upload the code, and open the Serial Monitor.

safety: Unplug the USB cable before changing any wires.
Double-check 5V and GND are never wired directly together (a short circuit).

spec.title: Read light levels with a photoresistor (LDR)

steps.text: Connect one leg of the photoresistor to 5V.
steps.tip: A photoresistor works either way round.

steps.text: Connect its other leg to A0.
Also connect one end of the 10 kΩ resistor to A0 (on a breadboard, put it in the same row as the photoresistor's leg).
Connect the resistor's other end to GND.
steps.tip: The two parts form a "voltage divider": more light means a higher reading on A0.

steps.text: Upload the code and open the Serial Monitor; cover the sensor to see the number drop.

safety: Unplug the USB cable before changing any wires.
Double-check 5V and GND are never wired directly together (a short circuit).

spec.title: Make a beep with a buzzer and an Arduino

steps.text: Connect the buzzer's + leg (longer, or marked +) to pin D9.
Connect the buzzer's − leg to GND.
Upload the code: the buzzer beeps once a second.

spec.title: Connect a laptop to an external monitor

pins.label: HDMI port (or USB-C with a USB-C→HDMI adapter)

steps.text: Plug the monitor into power and switch it on.
Plug one end of the HDMI cable into the laptop.
steps.tip: No HDMI port? Use a USB-C (Thunderbolt) to HDMI adapter.

steps.text: Plug the other end into the monitor's HDMI input.
Use the monitor's buttons to pick that HDMI input. On the laptop, Windows: press Win+P; Mac: System Settings → Displays.
steps.tip: Choose "Extend" for two separate screens or "Duplicate" to show the same thing.

steps.text: Plug in the laptop charger; external screens use extra battery.

safety: Push connectors straight in; never force a plug the wrong way up.

spec.title: Set up a desktop PC

steps.text: Connect the monitor cable to the graphics card's port, the lower horizontal row on the back.
steps.tip: If the PC has a graphics card, the ports higher up (on the motherboard) usually show nothing: a very common mistake.

steps.text: Plug the keyboard and mouse into USB ports.
Optional: connect an Ethernet cable from the PC to the router for faster, steadier internet.
Plug the monitor and the PC into the power strip.
Flip the switch on the back of the PC's power supply to | (on), then press the power button on the front.

safety: Plug in power last.
Don't open the case while it's plugged in.
